ACERBIC: Sharp or biting in manner or taste.
Often used of criticism: an acerbic review.
ACOLYTE: Originally an assistant in a religious service.
ADIPOSE: Consisting of, or relating to, fat.
A technical adjective, as in adipose tissue.
ANODYNE: Something that relieves pain; also, blandly inoffensive.
A harmless statement can be described as anodyne.
APHESIS: Loss of an unstressed vowel at the beginning of a word.
The change from alone to lone is an example.
ATAVISM: Reappearance of a characteristic associated with distant ancestors.
Also used figuratively for a return to an earlier way of behaving.
AUTARKY: Economic self-sufficiency, especially of a nation.
Distinct from autocracy, which concerns who holds power.
BATHYAL: Relating to the ocean depths along the continental slope.
A term used in marine ecology and oceanography.
BENTHIC: Relating to the bottom of a body of water.
Benthic organisms live on or near the bed.
BROMIDE: A compound of bromine; figuratively, a tiresome commonplace.
A reassuring cliché may be dismissed as a bromide.
CADENZA: An elaborate solo passage, often near the end of a concerto movement.
It gives a performer room to display virtuosity.
CAESURA: A pause within a line of verse.
The pause need not coincide with the end of a printed line.
CALUMNY: A false statement made to damage someone’s reputation.
A formal word for malicious slander.
CHIASMA: A crossing of structures, such as nerves or chromosomes.
The optic chiasma is a crossing of optic nerve fibres.
CHICANE: A series of tight turns; also, deceptive trickery.
The road sense is familiar in motor racing.
CHIMERA: An impossible fancy, or an organism containing genetically distinct tissues.
The word also names a composite monster in Greek myth.
COTERIE: A small, exclusive group sharing interests.
Often used of literary or artistic circles.
DEHISCE: To split open naturally along a line of weakness.
A ripe seed capsule may dehisce to release its seeds.
DITTANY: A name for several aromatic plants, including dittany of Crete.
The Cretan plant belongs to the oregano genus.
ECLOGUE: A short pastoral poem, often taking the form of dialogue.
Associated particularly with idealised rural life.
ELISION: Omission of a sound or syllable in speech.
In verse, elision can help a phrase fit the metre.
EPIGONE: A follower whose work imitates a greater predecessor.
Usually dismissive: it suggests imitation without comparable originality.
ERGODIC: Having statistical behaviour in which time averages correspond to ensemble averages.
A technical term in probability and dynamical systems.
FARRAGO: A confused mixture of disparate things.
A farrago of excuses is an unconvincing assortment.
FULVOUS: Used in descriptions of animal plumage and colouring.
GIBBOUS: Convex or bulging; of the Moon, more than half illuminated.
A gibbous Moon can be waxing or waning.
HAPLOID: Having a single set of chromosomes.
Contrasts with diploid, which has two sets.
INCIPIT: The opening words of a text or musical composition.
An incipit can identify a work that lacks a title.
INSCAPE: The distinctive inner character or pattern of a thing.
Especially associated with the poetry and thought of Gerard Manley Hopkins.
LAMBENT: Glowing softly, or lightly playing over a surface.
Can also describe a light, graceful wit.
LIMINAL: At a threshold or transitional boundary.
A liminal state lies between established conditions.
LUCERNE: A forage plant also known as alfalfa.
Lucerne is the usual British name for this deep-rooted legume.
MORDANT: Bitingly sharp in humour; also, a substance that fixes dye.
The literary and dyeing senses share the notion of biting.
OBLOQUY: A formal noun, often encountered in historical writing.
OCELLUS: A simple eye, or an eye-like marking.
The markings on some butterfly wings are ocelli.
PALUDAL: Relating to marshes or marshy ground.
A specialised adjective used in environmental description.
PERIGEE: The point in an orbit nearest the Earth.
Its counterpart, apogee, is the most distant point.
PLEROMA: Fullness, especially the fullness of divine being in some theologies.
A term particularly associated with Gnostic systems.
PROLATE: A prolate spheroid is longer than it is wide; an oblate one is flattened.
PROTEAN: Able to change form readily; remarkably versatile.
A protean talent resists being confined to one category.
QUONDAM: Former; belonging to an earlier time.
An old-fashioned adjective: a quondam colleague.
RAVELIN: An outer defensive work, usually triangular, before a fortress.
It protects the main curtain wall from direct attack.
SAPIENT: More formal than sensible; related to sapience.
TESSERA: A small piece used in a mosaic.
TRIREME: An ancient galley with three tiers of oars.
The name describes its rowing arrangement, not three sails.
UMBRAGE: Usually in the phrase take umbrage at something.
VELAMEN: A spongy outer covering on certain aerial roots.
VOLUBLE: Describes fluency or abundance of speech, rather than loudness.
ZYMURGY: The study or practice of fermentation.
Used particularly in connection with brewing.
ABRIDGE: To shorten a text without losing its main sense.
An abridged edition condenses a longer work.
AFFABLE: Friendly, approachable and easy to speak to.
It describes manner rather than appearance.
AMIABLE: Amiable usually describes a person or their behaviour.
AMNESTY: An official pardon granted to a group of people.
It often concerns political offences or surrendered weapons.
ANARCHY: A state without effective government or recognised authority.
In ordinary use it can also mean severe disorder.
ARCHIVE: A collection of records preserved for their lasting value.
The word can mean either the collection or the place holding it.
BESPOKE: Made for a particular customer or purpose.
Originally associated especially with tailored clothing.
BUCOLIC: Relating to an idealised rural life or countryside.
A bucolic scene is peacefully pastoral.
CANDOUR: The quality of being open and honest.
This is the usual British spelling; American English favours candor.
CAPRICE: A sudden and unpredictable change of mind or mood.
It can also name a lively, freely formed piece of music.
CLARITY: The quality of being clear, coherent or easy to understand.
It may describe thought, writing, sound or appearance.
CORSAIR: A pirate or privateer, especially one operating in the Mediterranean.
The word also appears in the names of several ships and aircraft.
CYNICAL: Distrustful of people’s motives or doubtful about sincerity.
A cynical remark assumes self-interest behind an action.
DECORUM: Behaviour considered proper for a particular situation.
To observe decorum is to respect social convention.
DEFUNCT: No longer existing, operating or in use.
Often applied to organisations, publications or machinery.
DYNAMIC: Characterised by energy, activity or continuing change.
In physics, dynamics concerns forces and motion.
EMPATHY: The ability to understand and share another person’s feelings.
It differs from sympathy, which need not involve the same perspective.
ENTROPY: A measure of disorder or unavailable energy in a system.
The word is also used figuratively for gradual decline into disorder.
EPITHET: A descriptive word or phrase attached to a person or thing.
It may be admiring, neutral or insulting depending on context.
EQUINOX: Either of the two times each year when day and night are nearly equal.
They occur as the Sun crosses the celestial equator.
EUPHONY: A pleasing or harmonious combination of sounds.
Writers may choose words for euphony as well as meaning.
EXCERPT: A short passage taken from a longer work.
The word can be a noun or a verb.
FURTIVE: Attempting to avoid notice, usually because of guilt or caution.
A furtive glance is quick and secretive.
GARNISH: To decorate or finish food with an additional ingredient.
In legal use, the verb has a separate meaning involving money or property.
HALCYON: Calm, peaceful and often remembered as especially happy.
Halcyon days are an idealised period in the past.
INFERNO: A very large and fiercely burning fire.
The capitalised form is the first part of Dante’s Divine Comedy.
JOURNEY: An act of travelling from one place to another.
It is also commonly used for a long process of change or discovery.
KINETIC: Kinetic energy is the energy an object has because it is moving.
LACONIC: The word comes from Laconia, the region associated with terse Spartan speech.
MALAISE: A general feeling of discomfort, unease or illness.
It can describe either a person or a wider social mood.
NOMADIC: Moving from place to place rather than remaining settled.
It may describe peoples, animals or a way of life.
PARABLE: A short story used to illustrate a moral or spiritual lesson.
Its point is carried by analogy rather than direct argument.
PARADOX: A statement or situation that appears contradictory but may reveal a truth.
Some paradoxes expose a flaw in the assumptions behind them.
PENSIVE: The word often suggests a slightly melancholy mood.
PHANTOM: A ghost, apparition or something present only in appearance.
It can also describe a sensation felt without an external cause.
PORTENT: A sign or warning that something significant may happen.
It often carries an ominous implication.
PRELUDE: An introductory piece, event or action.
In music it may introduce another work or stand alone.
QUARTET: A group of four performers or a composition written for four parts.
The term is used most often in music.
REQUIEM: A musical composition or service for the dead.
The word may also describe an act of remembrance.
RISIBLE: Deserving to be laughed at; ridiculous.
It comes through French from the Latin ridere, meaning to laugh.
SUBTEXT: An underlying meaning that is implied rather than stated.
Dialogue can say one thing while its subtext communicates another.
TACTILE: Connected with touch or designed to be felt.
A tactile control gives clear physical feedback.
VIBRANT: Full of energy, colour or life.
It may describe a place, sound, colour or personality.
WISTFUL: Showing quiet longing, often for something past or unattainable.
A wistful tone mixes affection with mild sadness.
